What Pursuit’s $485 Million Business Says About the Economics of Attractions

Experiential attractions in busy destinations can grow without drawing bigger crowds. An operator can sell a better ticket, add a second experience, or give visitors a reason to stay the night. But outside theme parks and ski resorts, few public companies show what that business earns, or how much cash it takes to keep growing.

Pursuit Attractions and Hospitality is one that does. It runs the Banff Gondola, the Maligne Lake cruise to Spirit Island, and Sky Lagoon in Iceland, along with lodges in several of the same markets. Pursuit expects about $485 million in revenue in 2026. Excluding Flyover, the flying-theater business it sold in July, management expects roughly $460 million in revenue and $126 million in adjusted EBITDA.

Belgian Travel Industry Fury at ‘11th Strike in 11 Months’

Belgium’s airline and travel sector is demanding stronger safeguards against strike-related disruption after air traffic controllers helped bring the country’s airports to a standstill on Monday.

The Board of Airline Representatives in Belgium (BAR Belgium) described it as the 11th strike affecting Belgian airspace in 11 months and accused public-sector workers of repeatedly undermining the country’s international connectivity.

Air navigation provider Skeyes said it could not safely provide regular air traffic control from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. local time after some of its staff joined a nationwide demonstration against government austerity measures. Only emergency and other safety-critical flights would be supported, it said.

Brussels Airport said all arrivals and departures scheduled within that 14-hour window would have to be canceled, while Charleroi Airport said disruption would affect its entire Monday schedule.

New Webinar: Who Remembers the Traveler? Building a Connected Customer Journey in the Age of AI

Travelers now pass through roughly 65 touchpoints before booking a trip, up from 45 in 2018, according to Skift Research and McKinsey. Travel brands own only a handful of them. Even within those, sales, booking, loyalty, and service run on separate systems, so the traveler’s history rarely follows them from one to the next.

That gap is getting more expensive. Personal AI assistants remember what travelers prefer, and they increasingly shape where trips begin. Agentic AI gives travel brands a way to compete: their own agents, carrying a traveler’s context from first search to the moment a trip is disrupted. Phil Wang and Ronen Kadosh of ElevenLabs join Skift to break down how customer experience leaders can build a relationship that remembers the traveler.

This webinar will answer:

- What changes for the traveler when every interaction starts with their full history?

- How can you carry the traveler’s context across sales, booking, loyalty, and service?

- Should you build one connected AI layer across channels or add AI channel by channel?

- Should voice play a larger role in the customer relationship?

- Which interactions still require a person, and how do you hand off without losing context?

- How do you build the business case for a connected customer journey in 2027 plans?

- What should you require of an AI partner before committing?

The Pressures on Expedia B2B

Expedia Group’s B2B business, the engine behind most of its recent growth, is set to slow. Expedia’s chief financial officer blames a tough comparison with last year. A Bernstein analyst sees pressures that could last longer.

B2B gross bookings grew 19% year over year in the third quarter, and B2B revenue rose 23%. But when Expedia reported results on November 4, CFO Derek Andersen told analysts the segment’s growth would moderate in the fourth quarter. A year earlier, heavy marketing by some of Expedia’s largest partners helped push B2B gross bookings up 24%, to $8.7 billion, a high bar to top.

Andersen also noted softer demand tied to the U.S. election cycle, geopolitical disruptions in the Middle East and Europe hitting long-haul travel, and a fall sale that pulled bookings forward into Q3.

Cruise’s Hidden Middleman: What Filings Reveal About Private Equity Ownership and Profits

Many cruise passengers have booked through World Travel Holdings without ever knowing it.

The Florida-based company, which bills itself as the world’s largest cruise agency, runs online travel agencies like Cruises.com, franchises more than 2,000 largely home-based travel agencies under Dream Vacations and CruiseOne, and powers private-label cruise booking sites for airlines, hotels, and other partners.

The company is not public, and most of its financials are not disclosed. But regulatory filings in the United States and United Kingdom show its franchise network is expanding and its subsidiaries’ profits are rising as more people turn to cruises. That kind of growth has attracted private equity.

Mr & Mrs Smith Booked More Under Hyatt but Earned Less on Each Stay

Mr & Mrs Smith handled far more bookings last year than before Hyatt bought it, but earned less on each one, and its UK business posted a loss, according to newly filed accounts.

Smith Global, the UK company behind the boutique hotel booking site, made 209,565 bookings in 2025, up 41% from the year before, according to accounts filed with the UK’s Companies House business register. More than half of those bookings came from members of World of Hyatt, Hyatt’s free loyalty program.

Hyatt paid £58 million ($72 million) in cash for Mr & Mrs Smith in June 2023 to bring boutique and independent hotels into World of Hyatt, Skift reported. About half the collection — more than 1,250 properties — can now be booked on hyatt.com, Hyatt says.
